targetKeywords: accessible money lessons for children with SEND
title: Financial Literacy Activities for Children with SEND
metaDescription: Concrete ways to adapt money activities for children with SEND, covering AAC, switch and eye-gaze access, sensory load and processing time.

sections.heading: Start with an access check, not an activity
paragraphs: Before picking a worksheet or a game, the most useful question isn't "which money activity is best?" - it's "how does this particular child take in and give out information most reliably?" SEND (special educational needs and disabilities) covers an enormous range of children, so there is no single accessible format that works for everyone. A layout that works beautifully for a child who reads symbols fluently can be the wrong starting point for a child who needs real objects in their hands, and a screen-based game that delights one learner can overwhelm another before the money concept has even been introduced.

A short access check looks at three things. Communication: does the child understand spoken words, pictures, symbols, objects or written text most reliably, and how do they respond - speech, pointing, an AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) device, eye gaze, or a switch? Motor access: can they manage a mouse, a touchscreen or a keyboard, or do they need a single switch, eye-gaze equipment, or a person moving objects on their behalf? Sensory load: are there loud sounds, flashing animations or visually busy screens that will distract or distress before the activity's actual content gets a fair chance?

This doesn't need to be a formal assessment. Watching how a child already uses a favourite toy, app or communication aid for two or three minutes usually tells you enough to choose a sensible starting point - and you can always adjust once the activity is under way.

sections.heading: Teach one decision at a time, with symbols doing the work
paragraphs: Once you know how the child takes in information, keep the money concept itself as small as possible. A practical starting point: show two pictured items and a visible budget - for example, a snack at £2 and a toy at £6 against a pretend budget of £5 (this is a UK-style example in pounds; swap in your own currency and amounts). Ask the child to choose the item that fits. Keep the layout predictable every time, and give a clear, consistent 'finished' signal so the child always knows when the decision has been registered.

Where a child already uses a core-vocabulary AAC system, choose symbols that match their existing vocabulary rather than introducing new money-specific icons. If their board already has 'want', 'need', 'more' and 'stop', build the activity around those symbols instead of adding unfamiliar ones - the barrier you're trying to remove is the money concept, not the symbol set.

Once the two-item choice is solid, add a third option, then repeat the whole activity with a different set of pictures. If the child applies the same rule to new items without re-teaching it, that's a strong sign the underlying concept - not just this specific picture set - has transferred.

sections.heading: Concrete alternatives to speaking or writing an answer
paragraphs: A learner doesn't need speech or handwriting to show they understand a money decision, and treating either as the only valid 'answer' will undercount plenty of children who understand perfectly well. A few concrete routes:

Always record the decision and, where possible, the reason given for it - rather than scoring how the child communicated it. A child who selects 'save' through partner-assisted scanning has given exactly as valid an answer as a child who says the word aloud.
list: AAC selection: the learner chooses 'save', 'spend', 'need' or 'help' on their core-vocabulary AAC device or board, exactly as they would for any other message.

Switch access with scanning: set the activity so each option is highlighted in turn and a single switch press selects it. Use the scan speed the child already uses day to day rather than a new default - a scan that's too fast turns the task into a guessing game before the money concept is even tested.

Eye gaze: space the two or three choices far enough apart that a fixation is unambiguous, and use the same dwell time (how long a look must be held to register as a choice) the child's everyday eye-gaze setup already uses.

Partner-assisted scanning: an adult names or points to each option in turn ('snack... toy... save it'), and the child responds with an established personal yes/no signal - a blink, a sound, or a hand movement.
Objects: the learner physically moves a coin, token or picture card into a 'spend' or 'save' tray.

sections.heading: Reduce sensory load and allow more processing time
paragraphs: Feedback that's calm and specific works better than feedback that's loud and celebratory. Instead of a fanfare for every correct tap, a short neutral confirmation - 'You chose the £3 item. £2 left' - gives the information without adding sensory noise. Build in a retry that carries no penalty, and give the learner (or their supporting adult) a way to turn off animation and narration before the activity starts, not as something they have to discover or ask for part-way through.

Processing time matters at least as much as sensory load. Many children with SEND need considerably longer than the 'think time' an activity assumes by default. A practical approach is to wait in silence for a genuine eight to ten seconds after asking a question before repeating or rephrasing it - rephrasing too quickly can itself become the real barrier, more than the money concept ever was. It's worth writing that pause into your own plan explicitly, because in practice it's very easy to fill the silence without noticing.

For the same reason, leave out timed elements - countdown clocks, response-speed scoring - entirely for first-pass teaching of a new money concept. They measure processing speed, not financial understanding, and for many learners the two are only loosely related.

sections.heading: Worked example: a decision the child can explain
paragraphs: A learner chooses between a pictured £2 snack and a £6 toy against a visible £5 pretend budget (a UK-style example in pounds - adapt the currency for your context). Start with just the two cards and a visible number line showing the £5 limit. Offer whichever access route matches the individual check from the first step - a switch-accessible selection, an AAC response, eye gaze, or partner-assisted scanning. Once the child is choosing confidently, swap in new pictures and a new amount to see whether they apply the same budget rule to unfamiliar items, rather than having simply memorised this one pairing.

sections.heading: Facilitator's step-by-step plan
list: Run a short, informal access check: preferred communication method, motor access, and any sensory sensitivities, before choosing the activity format.
Set up one clear instruction, a predictable sequence, and a quiet mode (no sound, no animation) that's available from the start, not added later.
Model the decision once yourself, then give a practice turn that isn't scored.
Ask the question, then wait a genuine eight to ten seconds in silence before repeating or rephrasing it.
Change the pictures and the amounts while keeping the underlying money concept the same, to test whether the idea has transferred.

sections.heading: How to check understanding
paragraphs: The clearest sign of real understanding is that the same decision holds up when something irrelevant changes - the setting, the materials, or the adult asking. Try the same budget decision with physical tokens instead of pictures, in a different room, or with a different familiar adult leading it. If the response changes only because one of those surface details changed, the barrier is probably environmental or interface-related rather than a gap in the money concept itself.

It's also worth noting whether a correct response needed a prompt, a model, or came independently, and writing that down rather than only recording whether the answer was right. A learner who reliably chooses the same option regardless of who is asking, and without a repeated prompt, is showing understanding that doesn't depend on one particular person's style of asking.

sections.heading: Common teaching mistakes to avoid
list: Don't equate absence of speech with absence of understanding - a non-verbal response through AAC, a switch, or eye gaze can be exactly as valid.
Don't assume one sensory design - bright colours, celebratory sounds, fast animation - is universally accessible. What one learner finds motivating, another finds overwhelming.
Don't read a longer processing time as confusion. Waiting it out is usually more informative than repeating the question.
Don't require a written or spoken explanation as the only acceptable proof of understanding when the activity itself didn't need one.

sections.heading: Try this next
paragraphs: Choose one activity from this guide and repeat it with a different fictional example and a different access route - pictures instead of objects, or an AAC response instead of pointing. Ask the child to show their choice using whichever method suits them best, and keep any real family financial details private; fictional names and amounts work just as well for practice.

sections.heading: Editorial references
paragraphs: General guidance on introducing money concepts to children, including keeping early activities concrete and goal-based, draws on the approach set out by the UK's Money and Pensions Service in its work on children and young people's financial education: https://maps.org.uk/en/our-work/children-and-young-people.

faqs.question: How long should one of these activities take?
faqs.answer: Start with a short session of around ten to fifteen minutes, and let the learner's attention and access needs set the real length rather than a fixed clock - for some children that will mean stopping sooner, for others it will mean several short repeats across a day. This is a practical starting point, not a research-established optimum.

faqs.question: What if the child gives an unexpected answer?
faqs.answer: Ask for the reason behind the choice if they can give one, check that the instruction itself was understood (not just the money concept), and try a fresh example before assuming the concept hasn't landed. Avoid treating speed or spoken fluency as a stand-in for financial understanding - a slow, non-verbal answer can be just as sound as a fast spoken one.

faqs.question: Do I need specialist AAC training to run these activities?
faqs.answer: No. You mainly need to know the symbols and access method the child already uses day to day, and to build the money activity around that existing system rather than introducing a new one. Where a speech and language therapist or AAC specialist already supports the child, it's worth checking the vocabulary you're planning to use with them, but a parent or teacher who already supports the child's communication can adapt these activities without new equipment.

faqs.question: The child's needs seem to vary from day to day - how do I plan for that?
faqs.answer: Build flexibility in rather than picking one fixed format. Having the same concept available two ways - say, pictures plus objects, or screen-based plus a physical tray - means you can offer whichever route suits the child on a given day without redesigning the activity each time.
